questions.q: Define Satyagraha and state its literal meaning.
questions.a: Satyagraha means "holding onto truth" (Satya = truth, Agraha = firm insistence). It is a method of non-violent resistance where the practitioner refuses to cooperate with injustice while willingly accepting suffering, aiming to awaken the opponent's conscience. A wrong answer (e.g., "passive resistance" or "peaceful protest") reveals confusion between Satyagraha as a moral philosophy and tactical non-violence.

questions.q: Explain why Gandhi distinguished Satyagraha from "passive resistance" and "pacifism".
questions.a: Gandhi rejected "passive resistance" because it implies weakness and may harbor violence in intent; he rejected "pacifism" because it is a personal moral stance, not a political strategy. Satyagraha is active, requires courage, and seeks to convert the opponent through self-suffering. A wrong answer (e.g., "they are the same") shows failure to grasp the strategic and ethical uniqueness of Satyagraha as a weapon of the strong.

questions.q: A student argues: "Satyagraha only worked because the British had a conscience. It would fail against a ruthless dictator." Apply Gandhi's logic to evaluate this claim.
questions.a: Gandhi argued Satyagraha works by exposing the moral bankruptcy of oppression — even a ruthless ruler needs legitimacy and cooperation. If the resister maintains non-violence, the oppressor's violence becomes visible, eroding internal and external support. The claim misunderstands Satyagraha as dependent on opponent's goodness rather than its ability to delegitimize power. A wrong answer reveals a mechanistic view of power, ignoring the political psychology of legitimacy.

questions.q: Compare the strategic logic of Satyagraha with Johan Galtung's concept of "positive peace" (from c11_ps_cbse_09_002). How do both address structural violence?
questions.a: Both go beyond absence of violence (negative peace). Satyagraha actively confronts structural violence (e.g., salt tax, indigo plantation) by non-cooperation, forcing the structure to reveal its violence. Positive peace seeks to remove root causes (inequality, exploitation) through institutional change. Satyagraha is a method to achieve positive peace by transforming conflict into moral confrontation. A wrong answer treats them as unrelated — one a technique, other a goal — missing the strategic link.

questions.q: Evaluate: "Satyagraha is impractical in modern democratic politics where elections and courts exist." Use the concept of "civil disobedience" vs "legal protest" in your reasoning.
questions.a: Satyagraha operates when legal channels are blocked or unjust (e.g., colonial law, apartheid). In democracy, it remains a last resort when institutional mechanisms fail marginalized groups (e.g., Chipko, Narmada Bachao). It is not a substitute for elections but a check on majoritarianism. A wrong answer either dismisses it as obsolete or romanticizes it as the only way, failing to see its conditional role in democratic theory.

questions.q: Design a Satyagraha campaign for a current local issue (e.g., water scarcity, waste dumping). Specify: (a) the unjust law/practice, (b) the non-violent non-cooperation tactic, (c) how self-suffering is incorporated, (d) the conversion goal.
questions.a: Example: (a) Factory polluting river violating environmental norms. (b) Villagers block factory gates daily, refuse to sell labor. (c) They fast in rotation, accept arrest without resistance. (d) Goal: Factory adopts zero-discharge technology; community gains monitoring role. A poor answer lists generic protests without the moral architecture — no self-suffering, no conversion aim, treating it as pressure tactics.
